> **Public version.** A generic week-by-week topic map, kept in "Week 1,
> Week 2, …" form so it stays useful across terms.

The table below shows the order the course builds ideas in, and which
weekly note page goes with each topic. Each note page is the main reading
for that week, with outbound pointers to OpenIntro IMS and ISLBS for a
second voice.

## Week-by-week

| Wk | Topic | Notes |
|---:|-------|-------|
| 1 | Data, evidence, and statistics | [Week 1 notes](notes/week01-data-evidence.qmd) — cases, variables, types; reading a small dataset honestly |
| 2 | Study design, bias, and causality | [Week 2 notes](notes/week02-study-design.qmd) — populations and samples, observational vs experimental, confounding |
| 3 | One-variable summaries | [Week 3 notes](notes/week03-one-variable-summaries.qmd) — center, spread, shape; tables and graphs for a single variable |
| 4 | Comparing groups | [Week 4 notes](notes/week04-comparing-groups.qmd) — conditional proportions, group differences, choosing the right display |
| 5 | Association | [Week 5 notes](notes/week05-association.qmd) — scatterplots, correlation as a descriptive number, the linear-only caveat, association vs causation |
| 6 | Confounding and multivariable thinking | [Week 6 notes](notes/week06-confounding.qmd) — confounders, stratification, Simpson's paradox, *alone* vs *after accounting for* |
| 7 | First-half synthesis | [Week 7 notes](notes/week07-synthesis-midterm.qmd) — Weeks 1–6 gathered into a six-step routine for reading any study from question to conclusion, worked end to end on two illustrative studies and carried to a third |
| 8 | Simple regression | [Week 8 notes](notes/week08-simple-regression.qmd) — the least-squares line, slope and intercept in context, residuals and the residual-plot reading, *R²*, extrapolation, influential cases, and reading regression output |
| 9 | Multiple / logistic regression interpretation | [Week 9 notes](notes/week09-multiple-logistic-regression.qmd) — adding predictors; the *holding constant* coefficient reading; adjusted vs unadjusted slopes; indicator variables; probability, odds, and log odds; logistic coefficients as odds ratios; predicted probabilities; odds ratios vs risk ratios |
| 10 | Probability as risk and diagnosis | [Week 10 notes](notes/week10-probability-risk-diagnosis.qmd) — probability as risk; conditional probability and P(A \| B) vs P(B \| A); diagnostic two-way tables; sensitivity, specificity, predictive values; false positives/negatives; base-rate effects |
| 11 | Simulation-based inference | [Week 11 notes](notes/week11-simulation-based-inference.qmd) — randomization tests, the null distribution, simulated p-values as evidence, bootstrap distributions, percentile confidence intervals, and reading StatKey-style output |
| 12 | Classical hypothesis testing | [Week 12 notes](notes/week12-classical-hypothesis-testing.qmd) — null and alternative hypotheses, the standard error and the *z* statistic, p-values and 95% confidence intervals for one and two proportions and for a mean, Type I/II errors with significance level and power, and statistical vs practical significance |
| 13 | Categorical outcomes | [Week 13 notes](notes/week13-categorical-outcomes.qmd) — counts, proportions, and rates; reading a two-way table with the right conditional proportions; a confidence interval for a difference in proportions; expected counts under independence and the chi-square statistic with its p-value; and association versus causation |
| 14 | Meta-analysis and forest plots | [Week 14 notes](notes/week14-meta-analysis-forest-plots.qmd) — how do studies become evidence? Effect sizes with confidence intervals; reading a forest plot (each study's estimate and confidence interval, the line of no effect, square size as weight, and the pooled diamond); inverse-variance pooling; heterogeneity and random effects; publication bias and funnel plots; and a responsible conclusion. The studies are hypothetical |
| 15 | Final review | [Week 15 notes](notes/week15-final-review.qmd) — what claim can we responsibly make? The whole course as one chain of reasoning from question to conclusion, worked on two studies and a screening test, with the course's common misreadings gathered in one place |

## How to use this schedule

- **Read by row.** Each row gives the week's topic and links to its
  weekly notes page. All fifteen weeks are live.
- **Read ahead, then back.** The topics are cumulative: each week assumes
  the one before it, and Weeks 7 and 15 are deliberate synthesis points
  that gather what came earlier.
- **Weeks, not dates.** This map is deliberately generic, so it describes
  the sequence of ideas rather than one term's calendar.

Section details and dates are set in the learning management system (LMS)
and the official institutional syllabus. See the
[Syllabus](syllabus.qmd) page for what this site does and does not cover.
